title: Research Progress on Molecular Reaction Mechanisms and Design of Vacuum Residue Hydrotreating Catalysts
content: Asphaltenes and metalloporphyrins in vacuum residue are large and prone to aggregation; consequently, their hydroconversion is constrained by both active-site reactivity and intraparticle mass transfer, while catalyst development has traditionally relied on empirical correlations. Based on the concept of molecular management in petroleum refining, this review examines the molecular-scale principles underlying the design of residue hydrotreating catalysts. Estimates based on the Yen–Mullins model and the Renkin equation indicate that when the pore diameter is approximately 9–10 times the diameter of the diffusing unit, the effective intrapore diffusivity can remain above 60% of its bulk value (approximately 18–20 nm for nanoaggregates and 44–50 nm for clusters). However, this criterion is sensitive to aggregate size and should be regarded only as an order-of-magnitude guideline. Density functional theory (DFT) calculations and scanning tunneling microscopy studies indicate that brim sites and sulfur vacancies at the edges of Ni(Co)MoS govern the hydrogenation (HYD) and direct desulfurization (DDS) pathways, respectively. Metalloporphyrins undergo demetallization through hydrogenation followed by ring opening, whereas competitive adsorption by basic nitrogen compounds and dehydrogenative condensation of aromatic cores are the molecular origins of nitrogen inhibition and coke formation, respectively. The relative advantages of Type I and Type II active sites vary with temperature and the rate-limiting step. The resulting relationships among key molecules, reaction characteristics, and design strategies provide a basis for the rational design of active phases, hierarchical supports, and catalyst grading.
